items.label: Kinds of work we take on

props.label: About Us
props.heading: A workshop run by the man who quotes your job
props.body:
Sonu Steel Furniture is a steel furniture manufacturing and fabrication workshop in Nagpur, run by Mohammad Arif. We are not a showroom reselling what a factory sent us — the measuring, cutting, welding, powder coating and fitting all happen with our own hands and our own team.

That is what makes made-to-size normal here rather than an expensive exception. A pharmacy with an awkward corner, a garage that needs a bench at a particular height, a school ordering benches for one age group — all of it is drawn, built and installed to the measurements of the actual space.

props.label: What We Do
props.heading: Furniture and fabrication
props.sub: Eight kinds of work, all made in the same workshop.

items.title: Shop & Pharmacy Furniture
items.desc: Counters, wall units, display cabinets and drawer banks, planned around your shop and installed as one fit-out.
items.body: Most shop furniture is bought piece by piece and never quite lines up. We measure the shop, plan the layout around how customers move through it, and build every unit to that plan.

items.title: Steel Almirahs & Wardrobes
items.desc: Two-door, four-door and wardrobe almirahs with locking rods, adjustable shelves, mirrors and lockers.
items.body: Made to the height of your room rather than a standard size, in the colour you pick, with the internal layout set to what you store — hanging, folded, files or all three.

items.title: Storage & Display Racks
items.desc: Drawer racks, crate racks, parts racks and open display racks, sized to your stock and your wall.
items.body: A rack is only useful if it matches what goes in it. Tell us the crate, the box or the part and we build the grid around it instead of asking you to fit your stock to a standard unit.

items.title: School & Institutional Furniture
items.desc: Desk-bench units, staff tables, storage cupboards and lockers for schools and coaching classes.
items.body: Institutional furniture is bought once and used hard for years, so it is welded at the joints and finished to be cleaned rather than cared for.

items.title: Workshop & Garage Furniture
items.desc: Workbenches, service counters, tool boards and heavy drawer units for people who work standing up.
items.body: Built to working height, with drawers rated for tools and a board that gets the spanners off the bench.

items.title: Custom Steel Fabrication
items.desc: Fabrication work to drawing or to site — structures, enclosures, gates, frames and goods lifts.
items.body: Where furniture ends and fabrication begins. Bring a drawing or bring us to the site; we measure, fabricate and install.

items.title: Steel Sofa & Seating
items.desc: Sofa frames, benches and waiting-area seating in powder-coated steel with loose cushions.
items.body: Seating that survives a public waiting room, with cushions that can be recovered instead of thrown away.

items.title: Repairs, Re-coating & Modification
items.desc: Re-shelving, new drawers, re-welding and fresh powder coating on furniture you already own.
items.body: Steel furniture rarely needs replacing — it needs a hinge, a shelf or a re-coat. Send a photo on WhatsApp and we will tell you honestly whether it is worth repairing.

props.label: Our Products

items.title: Medicine Rack
items.desc: Multi-drawer medicine rack in powder-coated steel, built to the depth your strips and boxes actually need.
items.body: A medicine rack lives or dies on its drawer depth. Too shallow and strips stand proud of the runner; too deep and the back of the drawer becomes a place stock goes to expire. We build the drawer bank around the sizes you actually stock, on a powder-coated steel body that takes years of being pulled open a hundred times a day.

items.title: School Desk & Bench
items.desc: Two-seater and three-seater desk-bench units with a steel frame and a hardwood top.
items.body: Classroom furniture fails at the joints, not the surface. These are welded at every frame joint rather than bolted, with the writing top fixed so it cannot work loose over a term. Sizes are made to the age group you are seating — a primary bench and a junior-college bench are not the same piece.

items.title: Pharmacy Counter with Wall Unit
items.desc: A matched billing counter and rear wall unit — drawers below, glass display above.
items.body: Sold as a pair because they have to line up. The counter carries the billing surface, the cash drawer and closed storage for fast-moving stock; the wall unit behind it puts everything else within one step, in glass so you can see what is running low without opening a door.

items.title: Glass Display Counter
items.desc: Long glass-topped display counter with a steel frame, for goods customers should see before they buy.
items.body: A display counter has to hold weight at the top and stay square along its length. Ours run on a welded steel frame with the glass seated rather than resting loose, in whatever length your shop front allows — including L-shapes for a corner.

items.title: Two-Door Steel Almirah
items.desc: Classic two-door almirah with a locking handle, adjustable shelves and an optional mirror.
items.body: The everyday almirah, made properly: a full-height locking rod rather than a single catch, shelves you can move as what you store changes, and a powder-coated finish that survives being wiped down. Colours are yours to pick.

items.title: Workshop Workbench
items.desc: Heavy workbench with a drawer bank below and a perforated tool board behind.
items.body: Built for a bench that gets stood on. Thick top, drawers on runners rated for tools rather than paper, and a pegboard back so spanners live on the wall instead of in a pile. Height is set to the people who will use it.

items.title: Service Counter with Tool Board
items.desc: Service-bay counter with a machine mount, drawers and an upright tool panel.
items.body: Where the job card gets written and the tools live. The upright panel keeps the bench clear, the drawer bank takes the consumables, and the mount is made for the specific machine you run — tell us which one.

items.title: Glass Display Cabinet
items.desc: Floor-standing glass cabinet with sliding doors and adjustable glass shelves.
items.body: Sliding rather than hinged, because a shop aisle rarely has room for a door to swing. Glass shelves are adjustable across the height, and the frame is powder-coated so the cabinet keeps its colour under shop lights.

items.meta: For auto parts and hardware shops

items.title: Goods Lift Fabrication
items.desc: Fabricated goods lift structure and enclosure, made and installed on site.
items.body: Fabrication work beyond furniture: the structure, cage and enclosure for a goods lift, measured and welded on site. Site conditions decide most of this, so it starts with a visit rather than a catalogue.

items.q: Do you make furniture to my own size?
items.a: Yes — that is most of our work. Send the measurements, or a photo of the space with rough dimensions, and we will confirm what is possible and quote for it.

items.q: How do I get a price?
items.a: Send the size, the material and a photo or drawing on WhatsApp and we will quote. Prices depend on the size, the gauge of steel and the finish, so we do not publish fixed rates for made-to-order work.
Tell us where the piece is going and we will confirm delivery and installation when we quote. Large fit-outs and site fabrication are installed by our own team.

Powder coating comes in a wide range of colours — the teal, green, blue and maroon in our photographs are all customer choices. Tell us the shade you want and we will match it as closely as the coating allows.

items.q: Can you repair or re-coat my old furniture?
items.a: Often, yes, and it is usually cheaper than replacing it. Send a photo on WhatsApp and we will tell you honestly whether it is worth doing.

items.q: How long does an order take?
items.a: It depends on the piece and what is already in the workshop. Ask when you enquire and we will give you a realistic date rather than an optimistic one.

props.heading: Not listed? We probably still make it
props.sub: Most of our work is one-off. Describe the piece and we will tell you whether we can build it.

props.label: Our Story
props.heading: We make it, so we can change it
props.body:
Sonu Steel Furniture works out of its own unit behind Satpuda Bar on Dighori Road, Aradhana Nagar, Nagpur. Mohammad Arif runs it, quotes the jobs and is on the floor while they are built — which is the reason a customer can ask for a drawer two inches deeper and get it rather than a reason why not.

The work splits roughly in two. One half is steel furniture: medicine racks and pharmacy counters, almirahs and wardrobes, display cabinets, storage and parts racks, school benches, workshop furniture and steel seating. The other half is fabrication — structures, enclosures, frames and goods lifts, measured and welded on site.

What ties them together is that nothing is standard unless standard happens to be right. Every piece is measured for the space it is going into, finished in the colour the customer picked, and installed by the same people who made it.

props.heading: What we tell customers before they order
props.sub: Six pieces of practical advice, written from what actually comes back for repair.

posts.title: How to choose a medicine rack for your pharmacy
posts.excerpt: Drawer depth, not drawer count, decides whether a medicine rack works. Here is how to measure before you order.
posts.body:
Start with the stock, not the wall. Lay out the strips, boxes and bottles you turn over fastest and measure the deepest one — that sets your drawer depth. Anything shallower and the drawer will not close on a full box; much deeper and the back becomes a place expiry dates go unnoticed.

Then count how many separate categories you actually reach for in a day. That, not the width of the wall, sets the number of drawers. A wall of forty identical drawers looks impressive and slows you down; a grid built around your own fast movers pays for itself in the first month.

Finally, think about who else uses it. If two people bill at once, the rack needs to be reachable from both sides of the counter, which changes where it can stand.

posts.title: MS or stainless: which steel for shop furniture in Nagpur
posts.excerpt: Stainless is not automatically the better buy. What each one is actually for, and where the money is better spent.
posts.body:
Mild steel, powder coated, is what most shop and home furniture is made of and it is the right choice most of the time. It is strong, it takes colour, it welds cleanly, and it costs a fraction of stainless. Its weakness is standing water — where a coating gets chipped and stays wet, rust starts.

Stainless earns its price where water is constant or hygiene is inspected: wash areas, kitchens, hospital and laboratory furniture. Paying for stainless on a bedroom almirah buys you nothing you will ever notice.

In Nagpur's humidity the practical answer for most shops is mild steel with a good powder coat, and stainless only for the parts that meet water. If you are unsure, tell us where the piece will stand and we will say which makes sense — including when the cheaper one is right.

posts.title: Powder coating and paint: what actually lasts in a shop
posts.excerpt: Why a workshop finish behaves differently from a painted one, and how to keep either looking new.
posts.body:
Paint sits on the surface. Powder coating is baked on, so it bonds and ends up thicker and harder — which is why it survives keys, crates and trolleys where paint scratches through to bare metal.

It is not indestructible. A deep chip is still a way in for moisture, so it is worth touching up early rather than after the rust bloom appears. Clean with a damp cloth and a mild detergent; strong solvents and scouring powder take the gloss off and leave a dull patch that never matches again.

An old piece that has gone chalky can usually be stripped and re-coated for far less than replacing it.

posts.title: Planning a pharmacy counter: billing, storage and the queue
posts.excerpt: The layout decisions that make a medical store faster to work in, made before anything is fabricated.
posts.body:
Decide where the customer stands first. Everything else — where billing sits, which side the card machine faces, how far the fastest-moving stock is from the person serving — follows from that one choice.

Keep the billing surface clear. A counter that has to hold the computer, the printer, the bill book and the card machine needs a dedicated shelf for each, or all four end up in the space you needed for the customer's purchase.

Plan for two people at the counter even if you are one today. Walking around each other in a one-person aisle is the thing that slows an evening rush, and widening it afterwards means rebuilding the counter.

posts.title: Looking after steel furniture so it lasts
posts.excerpt: Five minutes of maintenance a month, and the mistakes that shorten a piece's life.
posts.body:
Wipe with a damp cloth and dry it. That is most of the job. What does the damage is the water left standing on a horizontal surface overnight, usually after a floor wash.

Oil the hinges and the locking rod twice a year. Almirah doors that begin to bind are almost never bent; they are dry. A drop of oil restores them, while forcing them puts the frame out of square.

Do not drag loaded furniture across a floor. It is the fastest way to twist a frame that was perfectly square when it was installed. Empty it, lift it, or ask us — we will shift it for you.

posts.title: Made to measure or ready made: when custom is worth it
posts.excerpt: Ready-made is cheaper and quicker. Here is where it costs you more in the end.
posts.body:
For a single almirah in a normal room, ready-made is usually the right call. Nobody should pay a fabrication premium for a standard size that fits.

Custom pays where the space is awkward or the use is specific: a corner, a low ceiling, a wall between two pillars, drawers sized for your stock rather than someone's guess. In a shop it pays almost every time, because a few centimetres of wasted width at the counter costs you every day you trade.

The honest test is this: if a standard piece fits and works, buy it. If you are already planning to adjust it, cut it or put something under it, you are paying for a custom piece anyway — just a worse one.
